passage:
Monday. In art class, Akash noticed Aparna's drawing of a lighthouse and said quietly, “That's really good.” Aparna went pink and said nothing.

Wednesday. Aparna scored a goal at break. Akash clapped. “Great shot!” She smiled and said, “Thanks for saying so on Monday, too.”

Friday. Akash's pencil box fell and everything rolled away. Aparna helped him pick up the pieces. “Thank you,” he said. Later, Ms. Rana wondered whether the compliments were just friendly or a way of gaining a partner for the class project. Akash said, “No, I just liked them.” Aparna believed him.

qa.q: On which day did Aparna score a goal?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: Why might Aparna have gone pink and said nothing at Akash's first compliment?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and shy, since she had not expected it, though she remembered it later with thanks.

qa.q: What made Akash's compliments feel sincere to Aparna?
qa.a: He said them with no strings, repeated them over different days and thanked her when she helped, so his words matched his actions.

qa.q: Why might Ms. Rana wonder about the compliments?
qa.a: Compliments can be sincere or a way to gain favour, so context and reciprocity shape how they are heard, and she could not know Akash's reason from outside.

grounding: A child compliments a classmate's drawing and goal and thanks for help, and context shapes how compliments are heard.

passage: Jatin, you asked why I say thank you so often. Let me tell you about a boy in my class named Amandeep when I was twelve. One day Amandeep said to me, “That's a great answer!” after I spoke in class. I felt warm all day. Some weeks later, Amandeep asked to copy my homework and started saying nice things every day. I began to wonder: was it real? I asked myself whether he would say it if he had nothing to gain. Some were real, some were not. I learned to thank sincerely, and to notice whether compliments came with strings. Say thanks, but think, too.

qa.q: How old was the storyteller when Amandeep gave the compliment?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: Why did the storyteller begin to doubt Amandeep's compliments?
qa.a: The storyteller wondered whether the compliments were real or a way to get something, since they came with a request.

qa.q: What can a child learn from this story about thanking and complimenting?
qa.a: To thank sincerely and to notice whether a compliment comes with strings.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt if he was truly friendly and was doubted?
qa.a: He might feel hurt if his kind words were seen as tricks, which shows why context and reciprocity matter.

grounding: An elder shows that compliments can be sincere or a way to gain favour, so context and reciprocity shape how they are heard.

passage: The canteen was roaring, the bell was about to go, and Anirban had exactly one minute to find Aadhya. He'd been off sick all week, and she had copied her science notes for him, neat, with diagrams in two colours. He spotted her in the queue and pushed through. “Aadhya! Your notes. Thank you. The diagram of the heart was better than the textbook's.” Aadhya blinked. “You actually read them?” “Twice. I'd have failed the test without them.” She smiled, pleased and a bit pink. The bell rang. “Next time you're sick,” she called after him, “I'll do the maths too!”

qa.q: How long had Anirban been off sick?
qa.a: Anirban had been off sick all week.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when Anirban thanked her?
qa.a: Aadhya felt surprised and pleased, a bit pink, that he had really read and valued her notes.

qa.q: Why did Anirban's thanks come across as sincere?
qa.a: He named something specific, the heart diagram, and said how the notes had helped him, even in a rush.

qa.q: What would change if Anirban had only mumbled “thanks” in passing?
qa.a: Aadhya might have felt her careful work went unnoticed and been less keen to help next time.

grounding: Shows a child thanking a classmate for help with a specific, sincere compliment.

passage: In their Pune classroom, Tarun leaned over Bhavna's desk. “Wow, your drawing is amazing. You're the best artist in the class.” Bhavna felt her cheeks warm. Then he added, “Can I borrow your gold pen?” She lent it. The next day: “Your handwriting is so neat.” Then: “Can I copy your homework?” Bhavna frowned. Every compliment came with a request. On Friday, her friend Sana said, “I love how you did the sky,” and then just went back to her own work. That one felt different. Bhavna kept it in her head all day. When Tarun started his next compliment, she said, “Thanks. What do you need?” He laughed, caught out.

qa.q: What did Tarun ask to borrow after the first compliment?
qa.a: Tarun asked to borrow her gold pen.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she noticed every compliment came with a request?
qa.a: Bhavna felt uneasy and a bit let down, sensing Tarun's praise was a way to get favours.

qa.q: How did Bhavna respond to Tarun's next compliment, and why was it fair?
qa.a: She thanked him and asked what he needed, calmly naming the pattern without being rude.

qa.q: What made Sana's compliment feel different?
qa.a: Sana praised something specific and asked for nothing in return, so it felt sincere.

grounding: Shows compliments that are sincere next to compliments used to gain favour, and how context shapes how they are heard.

passage: “That goal!” Thomas jogged over, panting. “The way you curled it round the defender. How did you even do that?” Nazia grinned. “You passed it to me perfectly, that's how. I just had to hit it.” “No, the curl was all you.” “Okay, the curl was me. But thanks for the pass. And for staying back to practise with me on Tuesday.” Thomas shrugged, trying not to look pleased. “You'd have got it anyway.” “Maybe in a year.” Their coach, collecting cones, looked over. “Listen to you two. That's what a team sounds like.” Thomas held up a hand, and Nazia high-fived it.

qa.q: When did Thomas stay back to practise with Nazia?
qa.a: Thomas stayed back to practise with Nazia on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when shrugging off the thanks?
qa.a: Thomas felt pleased by the thanks but a bit shy about showing it.

qa.q: What made the compliments between Thomas and Nazia sincere?
qa.a: Each named something specific, the curl and the pass, and the praise went both ways without anyone asking for anything.

qa.q: How did the coach see the exchange?
qa.a: The coach saw it as the sound of a good team, with each player crediting the other.

grounding: Shows children complimenting a goal and thanking each other for help, with reciprocity making the praise feel sincere.

passage:
I'm Afreen, and last year I learned that the same words can feel different. When Rajni drew the banyan tree for our class wall, I told her, "The roots look like they're really moving." She went pink and said thank you, and the next week she helped me with my shading without being asked.

Then there was Sohail. Every morning he told somebody their handwriting was "amazing", and every afternoon he asked that same person to lend him their notebook. After a while nobody smiled at his compliments; they just held their notebooks tighter.

When Rajni thanked me for helping her study for the Hindi test, I realised that real compliments and thank-yous go both ways.

qa.q: What did Rajni draw for the class wall?
qa.a: The banyan tree.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel when Afreen praised the moving roots?
qa.a: Pleased and a little shy, as she went pink 😊, and grateful enough to help with the shading the next week.

qa.q: Why did Afreen's compliment land better than Sohail's?
qa.a: It was sincere and specific, about the roots, and came with no request, while Sohail's praise always came before asking for a notebook.

qa.q: How did classmates come to see Sohail's compliments?
qa.a: As a way to get favours, so they stopped smiling and held their notebooks tighter.

grounding: It is a child's reflection on sincere, specific compliments and thanks that go both ways, compared with compliments used to gain favours.
